materials.title: A. Planning a short walk and making flags
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A short group walk is easier to enjoy when its arrangements are clear. You do not need a complicated document, but a few shared decisions can prevent avoidable confusion.

Begin with the people who will take part. Ask about the distance and pace they can comfortably manage. ____1____ A route suitable for one confident walker may not suit a mixed group.

Check the route using current information. A familiar path may have a closed section or a changed entrance. ____2____ Memory is useful, but it should not be the only source.

Agree where and when to meet. “Near the park” leaves room for several interpretations. ____3____ A precise meeting point saves people from searching for each other.

Discuss what happens if someone arrives late or needs to return early. ____4____ The plan should identify an appropriate contact and avoid leaving anyone to guess.

Finally, treat conditions as part of the decision. A forecast or local warning may make postponement sensible. ____5____ Enjoying a walk includes knowing when another day would be better. A clear plan supports the group; it does not require everyone to continue regardless of what changes.
candidates: A. A shared arrangement is kinder than inventing one during a problem.
B. Some walkers keep photographs from journeys made years earlier.
C. A local shop may sell postcards showing the park in summer.
D. Cancelling one outing need not mean abandoning the activity.
E. Name a particular entrance or other unmistakable landmark.
F. Let those needs influence the choice before fixing it.
G. Look for recent notices about the paths you intend to use.

materials.title: A. Listening to a new language and measuring shadows
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Listening in a new language can feel frustrating when the speaker moves on before you have finished understanding. A useful practice session does not need to reproduce that pressure at every moment.

Choose a short recording with a reliable transcript. Listen once before reading it. ____1____ You will have a first impression to compare with the written version.

On the second attempt, focus on a small section. Notice where familiar words seemed to disappear into connected speech. ____2____ The difficulty may lie in the sound pattern rather than in unknown vocabulary.

Use the transcript to check a particular uncertainty. Do not simply stare at it while the recording plays endlessly. ____3____ A clear question makes the comparison more active.

Try listening again without the text. You may understand more because you now know what to attend to. ____4____ Improvement within a familiar recording is useful, though it is not the same as understanding every new speaker.

End by choosing a related but different short recording. ____5____ Some of what you noticed may transfer, while other parts will still need work. A realistic practice loop combines support, repetition and a fresh encounter, rather than expecting one perfect listen to prove mastery.

B. A fresh sample helps reveal what carries beyond the one you know.
C. Decide which phrase or sound you are trying to identify.
D. This keeps the first encounter from becoming only a reading exercise.
E. Replay that stretch and compare what you hear with what you expected.
F. The recording equipment may have a label showing its manufacturer.
G. Recognise that gain without making it a claim about all listening.

materials.title: A. Comparing arguments and making an index
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Two essays may reach different conclusions without disagreeing about every fact. Comparing them becomes more useful when you identify what each conclusion actually depends on.

Begin by stating each central claim in a sentence. Avoid replacing it with the strongest version you can imagine. ____1____ Otherwise the comparison may concern an argument neither writer made.

Next, distinguish evidence from the interpretation attached to it. A reported event and a claim about its cause are different steps. ____2____ Agreement about the event can coexist with disagreement about the explanation.

Check the scope of the claims. One writer may discuss a particular setting while another proposes a general rule. ____3____ Apparent conflict sometimes results from treating different levels as identical.

Look for an assumption that does important work. Ask whether the writer states it or expects the reader to supply it. ____4____ Identifying such a step helps explain why the conclusion seems persuasive to one reader but not another.

Finally, describe any remaining disagreement accurately. ____5____ A careful comparison can clarify the issue even when it does not settle it. Its value lies in making the reasoning easier to examine, rather than forcing two texts into a contest with a quick winner.
candidates: A. A longer essay may occupy more pages in a printed collection.
B. An unstated premise may be the point that most needs examination.
C. You need not manufacture agreement to produce a useful account.
D. Compare statements at matching levels before calling them contradictory.
E. Preserve the qualifications the writer actually includes.
F. Mark the move from what happened to why it supposedly happened.
G. The writers may use different titles for their publications.

There was also a difference ____6____ an event's date and the issue date of the newsletter describing it. We kept separate fields so a future reader could tell which one an entry supplied. Empty fields were left visibly incomplete.

The work did not remove every uncertainty from the collection. It made the route back to the actual pages clearer and recorded the choices we had made. That was ____10____ useful distinction: an index supported inquiry without becoming a replacement for the evidence it helped people find.

materials.title: A. Caring for a classroom plant and changing a play
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A classroom plant can be a shared responsibility without becoming a source of constant argument. The important beginning is to make the care arrangement understandable.

Find out what the particular plant needs. Different plants may need different amounts of light and water. ____1____ A single rule for everything green is unlikely to be enough.

Choose a suitable place with the teacher. A bright window may seem obvious, but temperature and space matter too. ____2____ The plant should not block a route or be placed where it is easily knocked over.

Agree who will check it and when. Avoid assuming that someone else has already watered it. ____3____ A small shared record can make the recent care visible.

Notice changes before deciding what they mean. A yellow leaf alone does not identify a single cause. ____4____ Ask for advice instead of trying several treatments at once.

Include weekends and holidays in the plan. ____5____ A school-week routine may leave a gap when the room is closed. Thinking ahead makes the shared responsibility more realistic and gives everyone a clearer role. The aim is to care for a living thing, not to reward whoever makes the most dramatic intervention.

materials.title: A. Taking notes at a talk and testing a model bridge
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A talk moves on even when your notes are unfinished. Trying to write every word can leave you with many sentences and little sense of the argument. A more selective approach begins with a purpose.

Before the talk, look at its title and any outline supplied. Ask what you hope to understand by the end. ____1____ You will still need to revise expectations as the speaker develops the subject.

During the talk, separate major claims from examples. A striking story may illustrate a point rather than establish a new one. ____2____ That connection is often more useful later than a detailed account of the story alone.

Use an unmistakable mark for something you missed. ____3____ Otherwise a guessed word may quietly become part of your record as though you heard it clearly.

Leave room for a question. It may concern a missing step or a term that was never explained. ____4____ Asking a precise question after the talk is easier when you know where the uncertainty began.

Review the notes soon afterwards. Add clarifications while distinguishing them from the original record. ____5____ A useful page shows both what you understood and what still needs checking. It need not look complete at the cost of concealing a gap.
candidates: A. Write enough context to remember why you wanted to ask.
B. The lecture hall may have several rows of folding seats.
C. Speakers sometimes travel by train to the venue.
D. A visible gap is safer than an unmarked guess.
E. Later additions should not be mistaken for the speaker’s exact words.
F. Record how the example supports the claim it accompanies.
G. This gives your attention an initial direction rather than a rigid script.

materials.title: A. Revising a claim and recording a local visit
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Revising an argument after criticism is easier when you distinguish the work from your wish to appear right. The purpose is to improve the account you can defend, not simply protect its first wording.

Read the criticism for a specific claim about your reasoning. A sharp tone may be unpleasant, but it does not settle whether the point is sound. ____1____ You can reject an insult without overlooking a useful objection.

Check the evidence named. Is the critic pointing to something you missed, or interpreting familiar material differently? ____2____ The appropriate revision depends on which problem you actually have.

If your wording was too broad, narrow it openly. ____3____ A qualification can make a claim more informative rather than merely weaker.

If the objection does not hold, explain why with the relevant evidence. ____4____ A reasoned response gives readers a way to examine your decision.

Finally, record a substantial change where readers of the earlier version can find it. ____5____ Quietly replacing a claim may leave the old misunderstanding in circulation. Revision is part of responsible reasoning when both the change and its basis remain visible.
candidates: A. Help those readers understand what has changed and why.
B. Separate the manner of delivery from the substance of the point.
C. State the conditions under which the claim can still be supported.
D. An essay can be stored in more than one digital file format.
E. Simply repeating your original conclusion will not answer it.
F. Some public discussions take place in buildings with large windows.
G. Distinguishing missing information from disputed interpretation guides the next step.

The account remained readable without supplying a confident cause for every alteration. We included references so another reader could revisit the same materials and make a different argument.
